tagline.text: A limestone cave on Panglao Island in Dauis, where sunlight pours through holes in the ceiling onto a green underground lagoon

location.label: Location
location.text: Barangay Bingag, Dauis, Panglao Island, Bohol

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱50–200 (entrance, swimming, parking and tricycle, per person)

children.text: A limestone cave about 100 m long in Dauis on Panglao Island. Sunlight enters through a hole in the ceiling roughly 1 m across, lighting up the stalactites and a green underground lagoon. It makes an easy short stop between Alona Beach and Tagbilaran.

Hinagdanan Cave is a limestone cave in Barangay Bingag, Dauis, on Panglao Island, just off the southwest coast of mainland Bohol. From the outside it looks like little more than a small ticket booth and souvenir stalls among coconut palms and scrub. Follow the concrete steps down, though, and you reach a wide chamber where sunlight falls through holes in the ceiling onto a green lagoon. The cave has almost no artificial lighting, and that natural light is its biggest draw.

The name comes from hagdan, the Cebuano word for ladder. The story goes that the landowner found a hole while clearing dead branches, threw a stone in, heard a splash, and set a ladder down to climb inside. The entrance now has concrete steps and a rope handrail, but the opening itself is only about 1 m across, so you still duck your head going in. The cave is thought to be about 100 m long. Getting here is easy: Panglao is connected to Tagbilaran by bridge, and Bohol-Panglao International Airport is on the same island, so you can stop by on the afternoon you arrive. The cave is small, however. A visit usually takes 20–40 minutes, or about an hour if you linger over photos or swim. Unlike most Bohol sights, which take half a day or more, this is best treated as a short stop between other plans.

The cave is one of the geological sites that make up the Bohol Island UNESCO Global Geopark, and it is listed in the Bohol tourism office's geopark guide. Like the Chocolate Hills, it sits on uplifted coral limestone, so it gives a quick look at how Bohol's land was formed. If you expect a large cave expedition you may be disappointed, but it is close to Alona Beach and fits neatly into a spare hour on Panglao. One thing to know is swimming. Swimming in the lagoon used to be popular, and staff on site often still charge a swimming fee, but Wikipedia and other sources say bathing is no longer advised because of pollutants carried in by karst groundwater. This guide therefore treats sightseeing as the default; check the signs and ask the caretaker on site before deciding to swim.

Visitor reviews are mixed. Some people enjoyed the light from the ceiling and the cool air, while others found it crowded, noticed a bat smell, or thought it was smaller than expected. You will be happiest if you go with modest expectations, as a cool place to rest during a day around Panglao. If you spent the morning swimming at Alona Beach, it is a good afternoon stop to cool off.

Beams of light enter through holes in the cave ceiling and light up the walls and the lagoon. The light tends to be sharpest around midday when the sun is high, but it can be weak depending on the weather, so do not count on a perfect scene. Looking up from beside the lake gives the best shot of the beams, but the edges can be slippery, so stay inside the railing.
Clear water pools in the middle of the cave. The green limestone on the bottom is said to give the water its green color. Clarity can change after rain.
Stalactites hang from the ceiling and stalagmites rise from the floor in many places. Touching them stops their growth or damages them, so look but do not touch.

The entrance, a hole about 1 m across, is a sight in itself. Steps and a rope handrail make it possible for children and older visitors, but wet steps are slippery, so take care. The steps down are not long but narrow, and in places people must pass one at a time. Let people coming down go first when you climb out.
It is a good place to escape the midday heat of Panglao. Many visitors say it is noticeably cooler inside than outside.
Some accounts mention sleeping birds in small holes in the ceiling. Sunlight is said to keep bats out, but one visitor reported a bat smell, so it may vary by season.

blocks.title: A base for a short Dauis route

children.text: Snack and souvenir stalls cluster near the cave, so you can rest with a drink. You can combine it with nearby Dauis Church for a half-day route.
A story says residents of Dauis used the cave as a refuge during World War II. There is little documentation, so treat what a local guide tells you as background only.
Set out from your Alona Beach hotel. The cave is said to open around
, so arriving just after opening makes it easier to avoid tour groups.
Buy your ticket at the booth and tie your shoes tightly. If you are not swimming, you do not need to pay the swimming fee.
Walk slowly down the concrete steps and make a loop through the cave. Take photos at the lake edge and under the ceiling opening, but do not go past the railing.
Head back out and rest with a cold drink at the stall.
Take a tricycle or taxi to nearby Dauis Church. Dress modestly.
Return to Alona Beach for lunch and some time on the beach. If you have time to spare, add a sea activity in the afternoon.
The light beams are best when the sun is high, but that is also when it is busiest. Decide between the quiet of early morning and the light of midday.

items.title: Continuing toward Tagbilaran
items.subtitle: From the cave to the city and its church heritage

children.text: Visit the cave after lunch. The light is usually brightest at midday.
Cross the Panglao bridge and head toward Tagbilaran.
Continue to the church heritage of southwestern mainland Bohol, such as Baclayon Church.
There are direct flights from Manila (NAIA) to Bohol-Panglao International Airport (TAG), taking about
1 hour 30 minutes
(1 hour 20 minutes to 1 hour 45 minutes) depending on the airline and schedule, so check when booking.
The airport is on Panglao, the same island as the cave. Take a taxi or a booked car from the airport to the cave; travel time depends on traffic.
You can also fly from Manila to Cebu and take a ferry to Tagbilaran. Check the ferry operator's announcements for departure times.
Flight schedules change often, so check the latest timetable before booking.
From central Tagbilaran, it takes about
15–30 minutes
by car across the Panglao bridge to the cave.
Buses and tricycles run from Tagbilaran to Dauis, but there is reportedly no regular jeepney to the cave entrance, so tricycles and motorbike taxis (habal-habal) are commonly used.
It is about
12 km
and
20 minutes
by car.
A tricycle is reported to cost about
depending on your hotel, and you will need to haggle. Many travelers rent a scooter.
The inside of the cave is less affected by weather, but in the rainy season rain can cloud the lagoon and make the steps more slippery. The dry season, November–April, is the safest choice.

Early in the day, just after opening, there are fewer people and it is cooler. If you want to see the beams of light from the ceiling, midday when the sun is high is better, but tour groups also increase. No time suits everyone, so choose according to what you want.

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary with local conditions.
The cave is close to Alona Beach, so most visitors stay at Alona Beach or along the Panglao coast. If you stay in Tagbilaran, allow time to cross the bridge.
A small stall at the entrance sells snacks and drinks. For meals, Dauis town and the restaurants at Alona Beach offer more choice.

Besides Alona Beach, Panglao has places to stay around the island and along the Dauis coast. There is no reason to move hotels just to see the cave; it is more efficient to combine it with other plans. Restaurants along the way change their hours and opening status often, so check recent reviews in a map app.
Wear flat shoes with good grip. Sandals slip easily on wet steps.
Keep your hands free to hold the handrail, and leave large bags and tripods behind.
A waterproof phone case or a strap lowers the risk of dropping your phone near the lake.
Wait until tour groups have finished coming down the steps and you will have a much more relaxed visit.
Some parts of the cave are dark, so bring your phone flashlight.
Bring cash for the entrance fee, and carry small bills since change may be short.
Do not touch stalactites or stalagmites.
Ask at the ticket booth before entering whether swimming is allowed and whether lifeguards are on duty.
Buy water and snacks at the stall at the entrance or bring them from your hotel. Do not leave trash in the cave.
The wet steps and narrow entrance are slippery, and some sources doubt the lagoon's water quality, so check conditions on site and decide carefully before swimming.
Wheelchairs and strollers reportedly cannot go down to the lagoon.
Paying the swimming fee does not guarantee water quality. If you have wounds or health concerns, just sightsee.
Do not dive, and do not swim after drinking.
Fees and hours vary by source, so check the latest notice before you visit.
The cave is narrow and dark, so it may be hard if you are claustrophobic.
In the rainy season the steps and entrance area are especially slippery and the lagoon can rise, so consider postponing on days of heavy rain.
Panglao's best-known beach, about
20 minutes
away by car. It has plenty of hotels and restaurants.
The island where the cave sits, with beaches and dive sites all around.
Bohol's central city, about
15–30 minutes
away across the bridge.
Known as one of the oldest stone churches in Bohol, it pairs well with the cave.
A church in the same town of Dauis. Dress modestly.
